title: Geometric Brownian motion
description: The test equation of stability theory, $dX_t = \lambda X_t\,dt + \mu X_t\,dW_t$, for each coordinate, with $\lambda = \frac14$ and $\mu = \sigma = 1$ (Drift & noise window: $u = \lambda x$, $s = \sigma x$; no potential). All 2000 particles start at $(1, 1)$. The exact solution is $X_t = X_0\,e^{(\lambda - \mu^2/2)t + \mu W_t}$, so $\mathbb{E}X_t = X_0 e^{\lambda t}$ and $\mathbb{E}X_t^2 = X_0^2 e^{(2\lambda + \mu^2)t}$. The SDE is mean-square stable if $\lambda + \frac{\mu^2}{2} < 0$ and asymptotically stable (almost surely) if $\lambda - \frac{\mu^2}{2} < 0$ (course notes, §4.2.3). Press play; step with → to stop at a given time.

questions.text: Pause at $t = 1$. What is the particle mean of $X^1_t$ (the Observable)?
Is this SDE mean-square stable, i.e. does $\mathbb{E}X_t^2 \to 0$?
Is it asymptotically stable, i.e. does $X_t \to 0$ for almost every path?
Type $\mathbf{1}_{x < 1}$ as the test function and run to $t = 4$. Which fraction of the particles is below 1 (the median of $X_4$ is $e^{-1}$)?

Most particles shrink towards 0, yet the mean grows like $e^{t/4}$ and the second moment like $e^{3t/2}$. Explain how both can be true, and what this means for estimating $\mathbb{E}X_t^2$ with a few thousand particles.
Set the drift to $u = -x$ (λ = −1). Which kind of stability holds now? Check it in the simulation.
